newsitem.title: INDIA: Israel sees Albright luring Syria to Mideast talks.
newsitem.headline: Israel sees Albright luring Syria to Mideast talks.

text.p: Israeli President Ezer Weizman said on Monday he expected U.S. Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright would be able to bring Syria into Middle East peace talks.

"Perhaps we'll let the lady try," Weizman told a news conference on the second day of his visit to Delhi. "I have full respect for (outgoing U.S. Secretary of State) Warren Christopher. But where he didn't succeed, the lady will succeed. She has the opportunity, because she has a more ripe situation now than Mr Christopher had."
Albright is due to take over on January 20 from Christopher, who was unable to bring Syria's President Hafez Assad into the peace process.
Weizman said Assad and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak were former air force commanders like him, enabling them to strike a common chord.

"I was hoping we would fly in a formation together, but it didn't help," he said. "I believe Syria will eventually have to talk, especially once the Palestinian thing is solved. She will not want to live alone. Syria is a proud, independent country with a proud leader -- I would say an outstanding leader."

Weizman said Israel's talks with the Palestinians about a deal on Hebron were not stuck because of Jewish settlers. "It is not a question of 400 Jews there, but to keep a footing in a holy city, sacred to Jews and to Islam," he said.
Israel and Palestinian negotiators hope to sign an agreement to give Palestinians control of 80 percent of Hebron.

Hebron, long a flashpoint of violence between Arabs and Jews, is the last of seven occupied West Bank cities Israel agreed to give self-rule to under an agreement signed with the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) in 1995.

Weizman told reporters after a ceremonial welcome at the British-built Presidential Palace that there were no easy solutions in talks with Palestinian negotiators over the elusive Hebron deal, but said he was hopeful about progress.

"It's not an easy problem. It's a difficult solution. But I am sure (there will be progress) in the very near future, I don't want to quote dates," Weizman said at the start of his first visit to India.
Indian Foreign Minister Inder Gujral told reporters that the issue was discussed by Israeli and Indian delegations headed by Weizman and Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
"Their response was positive. They said they are trying to restore the health of the agreements, the peace process," Gujral said.
He said India had also asked Weizman to help improve Israel's ties with Syria.
"We are equally keen that their relationship with the neighbouring countries, including Syria, should improve," Gujral said.
Weizman said no country in the Middle East wanted another Arab-Israeli war.
He said Mubarak was planning to settle several million Egyptians in the Sinai peninsula, neighbouring Israel.
"That is not the thinking of a leader who is preparing for war," Weizman said in a television interview shown on Saturday.
